newsitem.title: UK: British Airways slams hike in air travel tax.
newsitem.headline: British Airways slams hike in air travel tax.

text.p: British Airways Plc, the UK's biggest airline, on Monday slammed the Chancellor of the Exchequer's doubling of air travel tax, branding it as "extremely unwelcome" and "damaging" to the industry.

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke said in his budget on Tuesday that a 5.0 stg rate of tax on flights to European countries would be doubled to 10 stg, and a 10 stg tax for flights to the rest of the world would be raised to 20 stg.
While BA was damming, airport operator BAA Plc said the rise was "inevitable" and said it was neutral about its impact.

BA told Reuters it was calculating the impact the tax had had so far on passenger numbers. "The announcement is extremely unwelcome. It is an unpopular tax and penalises one of the UK's most successful industries. It will have a damaging effect on traffic," said a spokesman.
But rival transatlantic airliner Virgin Atlantic was more sanguine about the tax hike, which is not due to take effect until November 1, 1997.
A Virgin spokeswoman told Reuters "I think in the long term it won't have an effect. It's a shame it has increased, but its impact will be outweighed by demand to travel abroad."
BAA told Reuters the tax hike "was always on the cards," adding that the introduction of the duty had not resulted in a notable reduction in passenger numbers to date.

Chancellor Clarke said the delayed introduction of the duty would give holiday tour operators time to adjust to the new rates, and said that with business travel "soaring", 40 percent of the tax burden was borne by overseas travellers.
BAA's shares were up three and a half pence at 491 1/2 pence by the close on Tuesday, with BA shares ending down three and a half pence at 593.
